abstract: ArXiv:2606.31165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multipartite quantum entanglement plays a crucial role in the emergence of different quantum phases and their transitions in quantum many-body systems. It is of general interest to know what sort of analysis on quantum entanglement can bring us a profound insight to understand the rich dynamics of quantum many-body systems. In this work we study the characteristics of quantum entanglement in relation to [MATH]-ordered phases emerging under a varied strength of 1-dim Rydberg interaction. We propose an approach based on the structure of pair-wise entanglement across the Rydberg chain using two-qubit concurrence as an entanglement measure. We define an entanglement-structure factor via Fourier analysis of total concurrence at each site and address [MATH] phase transitions in comparison with the conventional order-parameter based on local density, i.e. magnetization. We also discuss how the required two-qubit concurrence can be measured in analog Rydberg atom arrays using site-selective erasure and parametrized laser pulses. Our investigation suggests that an entanglement-structure-based approach can provide a powerful tool in analyzing symmetry-breaking in quantum phase transitions.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement structure across Z_n phase transitions in 1D Rydberg atom arrays using pairwise concurrence and Fourier analysis.
motivation: Understanding multipartite entanglement in quantum many-body systems is crucial for characterizing quantum phases and transitions.
method: The authors propose an entanglement-structure factor based on Fourier analysis of total concurrence at each site, and discuss experimental measurement using site-selective erasure and laser pulses.
result: The entanglement-structure approach can detect Z_n phase transitions and provides a tool complementary to conventional order parameters.
conclusion: Entanglement-structure-based analysis offers a powerful method for studying symmetry-breaking in quantum phase transitions.

title: Pauli Weight Hamiltonian Term Selection For Optimized Machine Learning Based Quantum Error Mitigation
authors: Fadhil Fatih Shiddiq, Darell Timothy Tarigan, Hadyan Luthfan Prihadi, Jusak S. Kosasih, Yanoar P. Sarwono, Leong-Chuan Kwek, Freddy Permana Zen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning provides a scalable solution for quantum error mitigation. However, the selection of appropriate Pauli strings for inclusion in training data remains a challenge. Current methods rely on heuristic or uniform random sampling, requiring data for every Pauli string in the Hamiltonian, a process that scales linearly with measurements and grows with system size. To address this, we introduce quantum error mitigation with prior knowledge of Pauli weights (Pauli weight quantum error mitigation (Pi-QEM)), a systematic framework that selects training observables based on Pauli weight. By leveraging the relationship between variance and locality in parameterized quantum circuits, Pi-QEM trains on a small subset of dominant, low-weight Pauli strings. In numerical simulations of molecular systems on a noisy IBM quantum backend, Pi-QEM reduces ground-state energy estimation error by up to 34.01% using just a single dominant local observable, offering an efficient, scalable pathway for high-precision error mitigation on NISQ devices.
tldr: A machine learning-based quantum error mitigation method that selects training observables based on Pauli weight to reduce ground-state energy estimation error.
motivation: Current error mitigation methods require data for every Pauli string in the Hamiltonian, which scales poorly. The authors aim to reduce measurement overhead by selecting a small subset of dominant low-weight Pauli strings.
method: The method, Pi-QEM, uses prior knowledge of Pauli weights to select training observables, leveraging the relationship between variance and locality in parameterized quantum circuits. It trains on a small subset of low-weight Pauli strings.
result: In numerical simulations on a noisy IBM quantum backend, Pi-QEM reduces ground-state energy estimation error by up to 34.01% using just a single dominant local observable.
conclusion: Pi-QEM offers an efficient, scalable pathway for high-precision error mitigation on NISQ devices.

title: Theory And Practice Of Trotter Product Formulas For Quantum Chemistry
authors: Pablo A. M. Casares, William Maxwell, Danial Motlagh, Hitarth Choubisa, Zy Niu, Ignacio Loaiza, Jonathan E. Mueller, Arne-Christian Voigt, Juan Miguel Arrazola, Stepan Fomichev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trotter product formulas are a fundamental class of methods for Hamiltonian simulation, particularly attractive due to their low qubit requirements. However, they are often overlooked for use with fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, because of their perceived higher gate counts and the difficulty of estimating Trotter error. Here, we introduce Symmetry-Protected Randomized near-Integrable Trotter (SPRINT) formulas, a framework for building optimized product formulas for electronic structure Hamiltonians widely used in quantum chemistry. SPRINT integrates a generalization of classical near-integrability, randomization, symmetry protection, use of QROM, and other techniques into a thoroughly optimized methodology for Hamiltonian simulation. When applied to concrete simulation tasks, we find SPRINT leads to substantial reduction in gate count compared to previous approaches. Alongside SPRINT, we introduce and analyze a Generalized Rank Decomposition (GRADE) of electronic Hamiltonians that generalizes previous factorization methods. We apply these techniques to the task of simulating the X-ray absorption spectrum of Li[MATH]Mn[MATH]O, a candidate battery cathode material, leveraging recent advances in tight Trotter error estimation to carefully identify the best version of SPRINT for this problem. Using a Trotter error estimation tool developed in the PennyLane software platform, we show that SPRINT reduces the Toffoli gate cost by a factor of [MATH] relative to the previous state of the art for this problem, with a gate cost only [MATH] higher than qubitization, while requiring a dramatic [MATH] fewer logical qubits. These results establish well-designed Trotter product formulas as an attractive Hamiltonian simulation method for industrially relevant problems in chemistry and materials science.
tldr: This paper introduces optimized Trotter product formulas for Hamiltonian simulation in quantum chemistry, focusing on reducing gate counts and qubit requirements for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
motivation: Trotter product formulas are often overlooked for fault-tolerant quantum algorithms due to high gate counts and difficulty in error estimation; the authors aim to make them competitive with other methods.
method: The authors develop Symmetry-Protected Randomized near-Integrable Trotter (SPRINT) formulas, integrating near-integrability, randomization, symmetry protection, and QROM, along with a Generalized Rank Decomposition (GRADE) of electronic Hamiltonians.
result: SPRINT reduces Toffoli gate cost by a factor of 3.5 relative to previous state-of-the-art for simulating X-ray absorption spectrum of Li2MnO3, with gate cost only 2.5× higher than qubitization but requiring dramatically fewer logical qubits.
conclusion: Well-designed Trotter product formulas are an attractive Hamiltonian simulation method for industrially relevant problems in chemistry and materials science.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning For Individual Atomic Control And Cooling
authors: Matthew L. Peters, Guoqing Wang, David C. Spierings, Niv Drucker, Meng-Wei Chen, Audrey Bartlett, Isaac Chuang, Vladan Vuleti\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time feedback control of quantum systems is often limited by partial observations, nonlinear dynamics and measurement noise, which make accurate model-based controllers difficult to design. Here we show that deep reinforcement learning can cool the motion of a single neutral atom coupled to a high-finesse optical cavity using only the continuously monitored cavity transmission. We first train the controller in simulation and then transfer it to the experiment, where online fine-tuning adapts it to unmodeled experimental dynamics. The learned policy damps the atom's motion in real time and achieves a cooling time constant of 388 +/- 14 microseconds, corresponding to only two motional periods in the trap. It also outperforms a standard linear differentiator controller in cooling speed while maintaining comparable atom retention over a broad range of operating conditions. These results establish reinforcement learning as a practical strategy for feedback control in quantum-limited experiments where compact analytical models are incomplete.
tldr: This paper uses deep reinforcement learning to cool a single neutral atom in an optical cavity via real-time feedback control.
motivation: Real-time feedback control of quantum systems is challenging due to partial observations, nonlinear dynamics, and measurement noise, making model-based controllers difficult to design.
method: A deep reinforcement learning controller is trained in simulation and then transferred to the experiment, where online fine-tuning adapts it to unmodeled dynamics.
result: The learned policy achieves a cooling time constant of 388 ± 14 microseconds, outperforming a standard linear differentiator controller in cooling speed while maintaining comparable atom retention.
conclusion: Reinforcement learning is a practical strategy for feedback control in quantum-limited experiments where compact analytical models are incomplete.

title: Diffusion-warm Sampling Of The Xy Model Enables Fast Thermalization At Scale
authors: Sehmimul Hoque, Roger Melko, Pooya Ronagh
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a novel technique for scalable sampling of spin-system states with continuous symmetries using diffusion models. By applying our approach to the XY model, a fundamental continuous-spin model in condensed matter physics, we show that our technique addresses the shortfalls of the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) in generalization to varying system sizes. More specifically, we show that training a temperature-conditioned diffusion model on smaller-size XY model lattices enables the generation of accurate samples in larger lattice sizes. By tracking physically important observables of the model, such as spin correlations, our experiments demonstrate that diffusion sampling followed by a few MCMC steps reduces the thermalization time by an order of magnitude relative to the standard MCMC with random initialization. Our study provides valuable insight as to how generative models can be used to study continuous-state condensed matter systems at scale.
tldr: Uses diffusion models to accelerate thermalization of the XY model, a continuous-spin system, outperforming MCMC.
motivation: MCMC suffers from slow thermalization and poor generalization to larger system sizes; generative models may offer a faster alternative.
method: Trains a temperature-conditioned diffusion model on small XY lattices, then generates samples for larger lattices, followed by a few MCMC steps.
result: Diffusion sampling plus a few MCMC steps reduces thermalization time by an order of magnitude compared to standard MCMC with random initialization.
conclusion: Generative models like diffusion can efficiently sample continuous-spin systems at scale, providing a new tool for condensed matter physics.

title: Interplay Of The Channel-closing And Bound-bound Transition Resonances In Multiphoton Ionization And Harmonic Generation In Intense Laser Pulses
authors: A. D. Krupin, V. V. Strelkov, M. Yu. Ryabikin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, using a simplified model of the xenon atom, we numerically study the possibilities of efficient generation of coherent pulses in the XUV range through the resonant interaction of atoms with a moderate-intensity laser field, leading to the generation of its harmonics. We demonstrate the interplay of two systems of resonances affecting the harmonic generation efficiency. One is the channel-closing resonances, which arise when the sum of ionization and ponderomotive energies is equal to the energy of an integer number of laser photons. The second is the bound-bound transition resonances corresponding to an integer number of photons with a total energy equal to the energy gap between the Stark-shifted ground and excited states. The harmonic yields in the range of laser parameter values where both resonances occur exhibit a peculiar behavior, namely, near the intersection point of the resonances, a pronounced dip is observed, while the regions of increased generation efficiency due to the combined contribution of both enhancement mechanisms are slightly shifted from this point. We argue that this behavior, which is somewhat similar to the well-known phenomenon of 'avoided crossings', is associated with the formation of Fano-type resonant spectral lines. In contrast to 'avoided crossing' phenomena known in molecular physics, in the found interplay the contribution of one resonance system can be controlled, which is useful for experiments.
tldr: This paper studies resonances in multiphoton ionization and harmonic generation in intense laser pulses using a simplified xenon atom model.
motivation: To understand the interplay between channel-closing and bound-bound transition resonances that affect harmonic generation efficiency in intense laser fields.
method: Numerical simulations of a simplified xenon atom model under moderate-intensity laser fields, analyzing harmonic yields and resonance interactions.
result: Near the intersection of the two resonance systems, a pronounced dip in harmonic yield occurs, while enhanced generation regions are slightly shifted, resembling Fano-type resonances and avoided crossings.
conclusion: The interplay of resonances can be controlled, which is useful for experiments in coherent XUV pulse generation.

title: A Unified Perspective On Causality And One-Sided System Responses In Time And Space Across Physical And Fourier Domains
authors: Francesco Monticone Mohammadreza Salehi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The principle of causality has long been mathematically associated with the frameworks of Titchmarsh's theorem and the Kramers--Kronig relations. While these relations arise naturally in the context of temporal system responses -- ensuring that the effect of an applied field or force does not precede its cause -- they have recently been shown to provide a pathway for realizing one-sided system responses in a variety of physical settings. In particular, one-sided frequency responses and one-sided wavevector responses have been successfully studied and engineered, enabling the prospect of numerous applications based on the complete suppression of backward scattering. In this work, we present a brief review of causality and its connection to these Fourier-domain analogs. We then turn our attention to the only remaining setting in which a one-sided system response may be explored: one-sided spatial nonlocality. We specifically investigate the possibility of realizing a one-sided spatial response within the widely used framework of nonlocal flat optics, where we uncover fundamental obstacles that hinder the achievement of such functionality in these structures. This, in turn, raises an intriguing open question: is one-sided spatial nonlocal response merely incompatible with the specific platform of nonlocal flat optics, or is it fundamentally forbidden by nature itself?
tldr: This paper reviews causality and one-sided system responses in time and space, focusing on Fourier-domain analogs and exploring one-sided spatial nonlocality in nonlocal flat optics.
motivation: The authors aim to unify the understanding of causality and one-sided responses across different physical domains and investigate the possibility of one-sided spatial nonlocality.
method: The paper provides a brief review of causality and its connection to Fourier-domain analogs, then analyzes the feasibility of one-sided spatial responses within the framework of nonlocal flat optics.
result: Fundamental obstacles are uncovered that hinder the achievement of one-sided spatial nonlocality in nonlocal flat optics, raising an open question about its fundamental permissibility.
conclusion: The work highlights the limitations of current platforms for realizing one-sided spatial responses and suggests that such functionality may be fundamentally forbidden by nature.

title: Quantum Imaging Via Kurtosis-Difference Weighted Covariance On 2d Camera
authors: Zhe He, Yanli Shi, Hui Wu, Qun Cao, Weidong Zheng, Zheng Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Camera-based quantum imaging detects spatially correlated photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC). Conventional covariance methods typically require tens of thousands of frames to extract weak correlations from noise. While thick crystals can increase photon flux, they generate photon pairs from multiple emission positions within the crystal, producing multiple correlation centers with complex pairing geometries. In addition, conventional covariance methods assume a single pre-selected correlation center and cannot fully exploit these distributed correlations. We demonstrate that kurtosis difference, a fourth-order statistic measuring tail similarity, effectively discriminates correlated pixel pairs even when correlation coefficients remain low. Weighting covariance by an exponential function of absolute kurtosis difference can select symmetric pixels while preserving true coincidences. This kurtosis weighting automatically identifies correlated pairs within a broad search region and accommodates multiple pairing geometries without requiring precise correlation center calibration. At 5000 frames, our method yields a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) exceeding 7, whereas standard covariance remains below 2. Compared with standard covariance, the method reduces the acquisition time by 40-fold and could enable practical quantum imaging in sparse correlated-photon regimes.
tldr: This paper presents a quantum imaging method using kurtosis-difference weighted covariance to improve contrast-to-noise ratio with fewer frames.
motivation: Conventional covariance methods for camera-based quantum imaging require many frames and assume a single correlation center, limiting performance with thick crystals.
method: The method uses kurtosis difference, a fourth-order statistic, to weight covariance and automatically identify correlated pixel pairs across multiple pairing geometries.
result: At 5000 frames, the method achieves a contrast-to-noise ratio above 7, compared to below 2 for standard covariance, reducing acquisition time by 40-fold.
conclusion: The technique enables practical quantum imaging in sparse correlated-photon regimes.

title: Generalised Quantum Interference
authors: Sebastian Malewicz, Laura Serino, Marcelo P. de Almeida, Markus Rambach, Ming Su, Jihun Cha, Till J. Weinhold, Austin Lund, A. G. White
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference is one of the clearest signatures of quantum behaviour: two identical photons meeting at a beam splitter always leave together. Here we demonstrate that this symmetry can be broken. Using a programmable integrated photonic processor, we interfere imbalanced two-photon states on a variable beam splitter and show that the output state of quantum interference can be continuously tuned, reaching the extreme case where destructive interference suppresses bunching at one output port. The asymmetry creates a forbidden bunching channel: photons may exit together at one port or separately at both ports, but cannot emerge together at the other port.
tldr: This paper demonstrates tunable quantum interference with imbalanced two-photon states on a programmable photonic processor, breaking the symmetry of Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.
motivation: To explore and control quantum interference beyond the standard symmetric case, enabling new quantum information processing capabilities.
method: Using a programmable integrated photonic processor, imbalanced two-photon states are interfered on a variable beam splitter, and the output statistics are measured.
result: The output state of quantum interference can be continuously tuned, achieving extreme cases where destructive interference suppresses bunching at one output port.
conclusion: Generalised quantum interference with asymmetric states and beam splitters provides new control over photon statistics, with potential applications in quantum computing and communication.

title: Quantum Derivative Pricing For SPDEs Via Bdsde Representation
authors: Xinmiao Li, Yanqiao Wang, Rundi Lu, Zhengwei Liu, Jin-Peng Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31076v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study quantum speedups of derivative pricing for stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) models through their backward doubly stochastic differential equation (BDSDE) representations. We develop conditional and nested quantum-accelerated multilevel Monte Carlo (QA-MLMC) methods for estimating the resulting conditional and nested expectations, improving the sampling complexity of classical Monte Carlo methods from [MATH] to [MATH] within additive error [MATH]. We apply the framework to derivative pricing and sensitivity analysis, providing quantum-accelerated estimators for prices as well as first-order and second-order Greeks, likelihood-ratio and Malliavin-weight representations for Greeks, and Heston-type stochastic-volatility models. To enable efficient multilevel coupling, we construct a family of Forward--Backward Taylor discretization schemes for the stochastic integrals arising in the BDSDE representations and establish global strong-error order one convergence for pricing and Greek estimators. Numerical experiments showcase our schemes for first-order and second-order Greeks can reach the required orders for the full quadratic quantum speedups.
tldr: This paper proposes quantum-accelerated multilevel Monte Carlo methods for derivative pricing in SPDE models using BDSDE representations.
motivation: Classical Monte Carlo methods for derivative pricing under SPDE models suffer from high sampling complexity; quantum algorithms may offer speedups.
method: The authors develop conditional and nested quantum-accelerated multilevel Monte Carlo (QA-MLMC) methods based on BDSDE representations, and construct Forward-Backward Taylor discretization schemes for efficient multilevel coupling.
result: The QA-MLMC methods improve sampling complexity from classical rates to O(ε^{-2}) for additive error ε, and numerical experiments demonstrate the required orders for quadratic quantum speedups.
conclusion: Quantum algorithms can significantly accelerate derivative pricing and sensitivity analysis for SPDE models, with potential applications in quantitative finance.

title: Relaxation Of Incommensurate Structures Via Quantum Models
authors: Mengfan Tu, Huajie Chen, Daniel Massatt
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurately modeling structural relaxation in incommensurate systems is intrinsically challenging due to the absence of global translational symmetry. In this work, we develop a variational quantum framework for structural relaxation in incommensurate Schr\"{o}dinger models, where displacement fields are formulated on the configuration space and the electronic Hamiltonian is represented in reciprocal space. This yields well-defined relaxed energy, local density of states, and forces through thermodynamic limits. We propose an anisotropic scattering-channel approximation, and prove exponential convergence of the approximate equilibria. Numerical experiments are performed to support the analysis and show that the model captures domain-wall formation and its impact on the electronic spectrum.
tldr: This paper develops a variational quantum framework for structural relaxation in incommensurate Schrödinger models, focusing on domain-wall formation and electronic spectra.
motivation: Accurately modeling structural relaxation in incommensurate systems is challenging due to lack of global translational symmetry.
method: A variational quantum framework is developed where displacement fields are formulated on configuration space and the electronic Hamiltonian is represented in reciprocal space; an anisotropic scattering-channel approximation is proposed.
result: Exponential convergence of approximate equilibria is proven, and numerical experiments show the model captures domain-wall formation and its impact on the electronic spectrum.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a well-defined approach to structural relaxation in incommensurate systems with rigorous convergence guarantees.

title: Topological Phase Transition In Chaotic Optomechanical Systems
authors: Xiao-Jun Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hidden structures with well-defined predictability are uncovered in the evolution of a chaotic optomechanical system from the perspective of the [MATH]-machine. Tuning the frequency of the driving laser can switch off this predictability, and such behaviour corresponds to a phase transition that is deeply related to topological changes in phase space. The transition probabilities between causal states allow us to define an entropy (uncertainty) that serves as an effective order parameter. This phase transition can be readily demonstrated in currently available experiments by monitoring the quadrature of the optical mode. We hope that this work could fundamentally broaden the regimes of cavity micromechanics and nonlinear optics.
tldr: This paper studies a topological phase transition in a chaotic optomechanical system using computational mechanics and entropy as an order parameter.
motivation: To uncover hidden predictable structures in chaotic optomechanical systems and understand their phase transitions.
method: The authors model the optomechanical system as a ε-machine and compute transition probabilities between causal states to define an entropy order parameter.
result: Tuning the laser frequency can switch off predictability, corresponding to a topological phase transition in phase space.
conclusion: The phase transition can be observed experimentally by monitoring the optical mode quadrature, potentially broadening the scope of cavity micromechanics and nonlinear optics.

title: Atom Diffraction In The Strong-coupling Regime
authors: Carina Kanitz, Jakob B\"uhler, Fran\c{c}ois Aguillon, Vladim\'ir Zoba\v{c}, Jaime Glerum, Toma Susi, Maxime Debiossac, Philippe Roncin, Christian Brand
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analytic methods based on matter-wave diffraction are a cornerstone in condensed-matter research, providing access to static and dynamic materials properties down to the atomic level. In these experiments, the shape of the diffraction pattern is largely determined by the lattice at equilibrium whereas vibrationally-induced distortions are treated perturbatively. Here, we show that the perturbative approach does not hold for helium diffracted at kiloelectronvolt energy through freestanding single-layer graphene. In this case, we enter a new regime of strong coupling where the projectile strongly interacts with the electron density of several lattice atoms simultaneously, leading to phase shifts of several radians. In consequence, lattice distortions introduce a significant phase spread that cannot be described by the typically employed Debye-Waller factor. We show that the weak-coupling regime is retained for atomic hydrogen diffraction. The experimental results are supported by simulations, providing a regime-independent approach to describe the influence of phonons on atom diffraction phenomena.
tldr: This paper studies atom diffraction in the strong-coupling regime using helium and hydrogen on graphene, revealing that the perturbative Debye-Waller factor fails for strong coupling.
motivation: Understanding the influence of lattice vibrations on atom diffraction is important for condensed-matter research, but the standard perturbative approach may break down in certain regimes.
method: The authors perform experiments with kiloelectronvolt helium and hydrogen atoms diffracting through freestanding single-layer graphene, supported by simulations that model the phase shifts induced by lattice distortions.
result: They find that for helium, the strong interaction with multiple lattice atoms causes phase shifts of several radians, invalidating the Debye-Waller factor; for hydrogen, the weak-coupling regime holds.
conclusion: A regime-independent approach is needed to describe phonon effects on atom diffraction when the coupling is strong.

title: Boundaries In The Instantaneous Formulation Of Field Theories
authors: Silvester G. A. Borsboom
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study boundary conditions in GiMmsy's covariant and instantaneous formulations of classical field theories and show that the instantaneous state space in the presence of a constant Dirichlet boundary condition is a tangent bundle to the configuration space of fields satisfying said condition. We then study the instantaneous state space when only the velocity of the field is required to vanish at the boundary and show that this results in a sector structure, where each sector is a tangent bundle labeled by the configuration at the boundary. Taking the Legendre transform of this sectored state space yields a sectored phase space with leafwise canonical Poisson structures. We apply this to Yang-Mills theory with spatial boundary conditions and relate our results to flux superselection sectors. The sector-moving gauge transformations are not Hamiltonian because of the lack of a boundary momentum, prompting us to propose a novel definition of the asymptotic or boundary symmetry group as the quotient of the boundary-preserving Hamiltonian transformations by the trivial ones. The physical boundary symmetry group of electromagnetism is then shown to be a copy of the global gauge group even when all sectors are considered simultaneously. Conditions are discussed under which the same holds for non-Abelian Yang-Mills theory.
tldr: This paper studies boundary conditions in classical field theories using a covariant and instantaneous formulation, focusing on the structure of the instantaneous state space and its implications for gauge theories.
motivation: Understanding boundary conditions in field theories is important for defining the state space and symmetries, especially in gauge theories where boundary terms can lead to superselection sectors.
method: The author analyzes the instantaneous state space under Dirichlet and Neumann-like boundary conditions, showing it becomes a tangent bundle or a sector structure. The Legendre transform yields a sectored phase space with leafwise Poisson structures, and gauge transformations are examined for Hamiltonian nature.
result: The paper finds that sector-moving gauge transformations are not Hamiltonian due to missing boundary momentum, leading to a new definition of the asymptotic symmetry group. For electromagnetism, the physical boundary symmetry group is a copy of the global gauge group even when all sectors are considered.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous framework for boundary conditions in classical field theories, with implications for understanding symmetries and superselection sectors in gauge theories.

title: Non-Hermitian Rayleigh-Schr\"{o}dinger-like Perturbation Theory At Exceptional Point
authors: Chia-Yi Ju Wei-Ming Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a Rayleigh--Schr\"{o}dinger-like perturbation theory for non-Hermitian quantum systems at an exceptional point of order [MATH]. Working in the Jordan basis of the unperturbed Hamiltonian and employing a Puiseux expansion of the perturbed eigenvalues and eigenstates, we derive explicit recursion relations for the expansion coefficients. The corrections to the unperturbed eigenvalue in the Puiseux expansion govern the splitting near the exceptional point; the first two are obtained iteratively in two equivalent forms. One is given in terms of the perturbation Hamiltonian in the Jordan basis, and the other in terms of the generator that drives the eigenvalue evolution with respect to the perturbation. The latter constitutes the exceptional-point counterpart of a geometric perturbation method recently developed for the non-exceptional-point regime. Both representations are verified explicitly for the [MATH] and [MATH] cases.
tldr: Develops a perturbation theory for non-Hermitian systems at exceptional points using Puiseux expansions.
motivation: To provide a systematic method for analyzing eigenvalue splitting and state corrections near exceptional points in non-Hermitian quantum mechanics.
method: Works in the Jordan basis of the unperturbed Hamiltonian and employs a Puiseux expansion of perturbed eigenvalues and eigenstates, deriving recursion relations for expansion coefficients.
result: Derives explicit recursion relations for the first two correction terms in two equivalent forms, verified for 2x2 and 3x3 cases.
conclusion: The method provides a counterpart to geometric perturbation theory for non-exceptional points, enabling analysis of non-Hermitian systems near exceptional points.

title: Non-invertible Symmetries And Modular Invariance In Lattice Models
authors: Yacine Ikhlef
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider classical 2d lattice models with face interactions defined in terms of a fusion category. The symmetries of such models typically include an algebra of topological operators sitting on a closed path in the lattice. In the case when the face interactions obey the Temperley-Lieb (TL) relations, we present a generic algorithm to determine the decomposition of the transfer-matrix space of states as a direct sum of simple TL modules. We apply this approach to several examples, and analyse the action of topological operators. As an application, we compute the modular transformation of the irreducible TL characters at primitive roots of unity.
tldr: This paper studies non-invertible symmetries and modular invariance in classical 2d lattice models using fusion categories and Temperley-Lieb algebras.
motivation: To understand the algebraic structure of topological operators and modular transformations in lattice models with fusion category symmetries.
method: Develops an algorithm to decompose the transfer-matrix state space into simple TL modules and analyzes the action of topological operators.
result: Computes modular transformations of irreducible TL characters at primitive roots of unity for several examples.
conclusion: The approach provides a systematic way to analyze non-invertible symmetries in lattice models, but the results are primarily mathematical and not directly connected to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Vector Alignment In Matrix Lie Groups
authors: Congzhou M Sha
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The difference in gauge between two observers of the same physical system can be thought of as a group element acting on their common vector representations. Recovering that group element from a finite, noisy list of paired observations may be of use in both theory and experiment. The Kabsch and Horn algorithms efficiently align point clouds in [MATH], reconciling rotated frames of reference in Galilean relativity (i.e. [MATH]). In a previous work, we proposed an alternative Lie algebra method which extends to the Lorentz group [MATH], and putatively to all Lie groups. In this work, we report the explicit formulae for applying the Lie algebra method to the classical matrix Lie groups (general linear [MATH], special linear [MATH], special orthogonal [MATH], unitary [MATH], indefinite special orthogonal [MATH], symplectic [MATH], spin [MATH], special Euclidean [MATH]) over both the real and complex fields. The four steps (pseudoinverse, matrix logarithm, projection onto the Lie algebra, matrix exponential) are exact in the noiseless case. The only group-dependent step is the projection, which we show produces the unique least squares-optimal element of the Lie algebra whenever its image lies in [MATH] and its residual is orthogonal to [MATH]. Additionally, the Lie algebra method is optimal only to leading order for noisy data, so we refine it with a Newton-style correction. This correction matches the Lie algebra method in the noiseless case and direct least squares optimization in the noisy case, with performance between that of the Lie algebra method without correction and naive least squares optimization. The projections, their optimality, and the identity underlying the correction are formally proven in Lean~4.31.0 (with Mathlib 4.31.0), and numerical experiments are benchmarked in Julia.
tldr: This paper presents a Lie algebra method for aligning vectors in matrix Lie groups, with formal proofs and numerical benchmarks.
motivation: Recovering the group element that relates two observers' vector representations from noisy data is useful in physics and engineering, but existing methods are limited to specific groups.
method: The method uses pseudoinverse, matrix logarithm, projection onto the Lie algebra, and matrix exponential, with a Newton-style correction for noisy data; projections and optimality are formally proven in Lean 4.
result: The method is exact in the noiseless case and performs between the uncorrected Lie algebra method and naive least squares optimization for noisy data.
conclusion: The approach extends to all classical matrix Lie groups and provides a general framework for vector alignment, with formal verification ensuring correctness.

title: Compositionality Of Global Dynamics In Product And Skew-Product Systems
authors: Tony Wehbe William D. Kalies
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the compositionality of global dynamics through attractor lattices and order structures of recurrent dynamics in product and skew-product systems using Conley theory. For product systems, these structures can be characterized algebraically in terms of the structure of component systems, where we prove that the attractor lattice of the direct product of two flows is isomorphic to the coproduct of the attractor lattices of the component flows. We also consider fast-slow, skew-product systems that arise from singular perturbation of a parameterized dynamical system. These results provide a framework for decomposing global dynamics into lower-dimensional subsystems and suggest computational approaches for constructing Conley-Morse representations through composition.
tldr: This paper studies the compositionality of global dynamics in product and skew-product systems using Conley theory, focusing on attractor lattices and order structures.
motivation: To develop a framework for decomposing global dynamics into lower-dimensional subsystems, enabling computational construction of Conley-Morse representations.
method: The authors use Conley theory to characterize attractor lattices and recurrent dynamics in product and skew-product systems, proving algebraic isomorphisms for product systems and analyzing fast-slow skew-product systems.
result: For product systems, the attractor lattice is isomorphic to the coproduct of component attractor lattices; for skew-product systems, a framework for decomposition is provided.
conclusion: The results offer a compositional approach to global dynamics, with potential computational applications for constructing Conley-Morse representations.

title: Distributional Results For The Shortest Distance Between Trajectories Of Different Dynamics
authors: Romain Aimino, Th\'eophile Caby, Jorge Milhazes Freitas, Duarte S\'a Pinho
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish Extreme Value Distributions for the closest encounter between trajectories generated by different maps defined in the same reference phase space. For a class of strongly mixing maps, we show that the limit distribution depends on the length of the different trajectories and the co-dimension of the associated invariant measures. It is also modulated by an Extremal Index, that informs on the tendency of nearby points to diverge along with the evolution of their respective dynamics, serving as an indicator of their compatibility. We give a formula for this quantity for a class of chaotic maps of the interval and for the co-dimension in the case when the respective measures admit densities with isolated zeros and singularities. We present diverse examples of systems satisfying these assumptions and compute the different parameters modulating the limit distribution.
tldr: This paper derives extreme value distributions for the closest encounter between trajectories of different dynamical systems, focusing on strongly mixing maps and chaotic systems.
motivation: Understanding the statistical properties of close encounters between trajectories from different dynamics is a fundamental problem in dynamical systems theory.
method: The authors use extreme value theory and establish limit distributions that depend on trajectory length and co-dimension of invariant measures, modulated by an Extremal Index.
result: They provide formulas for the Extremal Index and co-dimension for a class of chaotic maps, with examples satisfying the assumptions.
conclusion: The work contributes to the theory of dynamical systems but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Online Tt-als For Streaming Tensor Decomposition With Incremental Orthogonalization
authors: Hiroki Takeda, Yuto Miyatake, Daisuke Furihata
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition is a powerful technique for analyzing high-dimensional data. Existing algorithms for computing TT decompositions can be categorized into two main types: conventional batch-based approaches and recursive online methods. In the context of streaming data, batch methods typically achieve higher reconstruction accuracy but often suffer from memory exhaustion, while online methods provide greater computational efficiency. In this work, we introduce Online TT-ALS (Alternating Least Squares), an algorithm that sequentially enforces orthogonality constraints. This approach allows for efficient and exact updates of the core tensor while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy. Theoretically, we prove that enforcing these orthogonal gauge constraints guarantees monotonic decrease of the local objective function and temporal smoothness. Computationally, our deterministic single-sweep update reduces the rank dependence from quadratic to linear, achieving an overall complexity of [MATH]. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing online techniques not only in terms of mathematical approximation accuracy but also in human perception-based video quality metrics. Furthermore, compared to recent deep learning-based paradigms, our algebraic approach achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude. Consequently, our method exhibits high computational efficiency and is suitable for low-latency real-time processing applications.
tldr: This paper proposes an online algorithm for tensor train decomposition with incremental orthogonalization, achieving high accuracy and efficiency for streaming data.
motivation: Streaming tensor data requires efficient decomposition methods that balance accuracy and memory usage; existing batch methods are memory-intensive while online methods sacrifice accuracy.
method: The authors introduce Online TT-ALS, which enforces orthogonal gauge constraints sequentially, enabling exact core tensor updates with a deterministic single-sweep that reduces rank dependence from quadratic to linear.
result: The method outperforms existing online techniques in reconstruction accuracy and video quality metrics, and achieves orders-of-magnitude speedup over deep learning approaches.
conclusion: Online TT-ALS is suitable for low-latency real-time processing of high-dimensional streaming data.

title: Fundamental Limits Of Quantized Mimo Isac Under Gaussian Signaling
authors: Hossein Atrsaei, Mireille Sarkiss, Mich\`ele Wigger
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a quantized multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system in which the communication and sensing receivers each apply analog spatial combining followed by scalar subtractive dithered quantization. This quantization model leads to an additive effective-noise representation with non-Gaussian noise. We derive upper and lower bounds on the capacity of this channel. Numerical results show that these bounds are tight at low signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and saturate at high SNR due to finite-resolution quantization. They also show that, despite the effective noise being non-Gaussian, independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) isotropic Gaussian signaling achieves rates close to capacity. Focusing on i.i.d. Gaussian signaling, this paper also presents a closed-form expression for the linear minimum mean-squared error (LMMSE) achieved under a Kronecker sensing-channel model. Numerical results show that the LMMSE also saturates at high SNR, where the saturation level increases as the spatial combining ratio decreases, and for combining ratios below one, saturation occurs even without quantization.
tldr: This paper studies fundamental limits of quantized MIMO integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems under Gaussian signaling.
motivation: To understand the performance limits of ISAC systems with finite-resolution quantization, which is important for practical implementations.
method: Derives upper and lower bounds on capacity for a quantized MIMO ISAC channel with analog spatial combining and subtractive dithered quantization, and analyzes LMMSE under a Kronecker model.
result: Bounds are tight at low SNR and saturate at high SNR; i.i.d. Gaussian signaling is near-optimal; LMMSE saturates at high SNR with saturation level depending on combining ratio.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical insights into the trade-offs in quantized MIMO ISAC, but is primarily an engineering communication problem without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Gabor Orthonormal Bases With Maximal Localization And Gabor Frame Operator On Local Fields
authors: Qaiser Jahan Kumar Abhinav
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide an explicit construction of a Gabor orthonormal bases for a local field [MATH] that provides maximal localization in both time and frequency. Such a localization is not true in case of [MATH] due to the uncertainty principle. In particular, we construct examples of functions [MATH] such that the support of the ambiguity function of [MATH] is of minimum measure. Moreover, we establish a quantitative uncertainty principle for local fields, which follows as a consequence of Lieb's inequalities for general locally compact abelian group. In addition, we develop fundamental operator representations for Gabor systems defined over local fields.
tldr: This paper constructs Gabor orthonormal bases with maximal localization on local fields and proves a quantitative uncertainty principle.
motivation: To achieve maximal time-frequency localization on local fields, which is impossible on ℝ due to the uncertainty principle.
method: Explicit construction of functions with minimal ambiguity function support; use of Lieb's inequalities for locally compact abelian groups.
result: Construction of Gabor orthonormal bases with maximal localization; a quantitative uncertainty principle for local fields.
conclusion: Local fields allow Gabor bases with better localization than ℝ, with implications for signal processing on such groups.

title: The Geometry Of Statistical Feature Learning In Mean-Field Langevin Dynamics
authors: Zong Shang, Tomoya Wakayama, Guillaume Lecu\'e, Taiji Suzuki
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a geometric formulation of statistical feature learning for supervised regression. Feature learning is defined through a base--fiber decomposition: the base is the feature-side geometry produced by training, and the fiber is the learned feature space where estimation is performed. We prove this property for spherical mean-field Langevin dynamics, viewed as the Wasserstein gradient flow of a negative entropy-regularized empirical risk. In Gaussian multi-index models, the low-temperature stationary distribution concentrates near the hidden indices, forms a multi-spike structure, and yields parameter recovery with high probability, even though negative entropy regularization penalizes concentration. This concentration has a sharp transition at temperature [MATH]. In Gaussian single-index models, the stationary measure satisfies a L\'evy--Milman concentration property, with parity determining whether it lives on [MATH] or [MATH]. The induced learned feature space aligns the regression signal and yields rates [MATH] and [MATH], up to logarithmic factors.
tldr: This paper studies statistical feature learning in mean-field Langevin dynamics using a geometric formulation, focusing on supervised regression and Gaussian multi-index models.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how feature learning emerges in high-dimensional regression and to characterize the geometry of learned feature spaces.
method: They introduce a base-fiber decomposition and analyze spherical mean-field Langevin dynamics as a Wasserstein gradient flow of entropy-regularized empirical risk, studying stationary distributions in Gaussian multi-index and single-index models.
result: They show that low-temperature stationary distributions concentrate near hidden indices, forming a multi-spike structure, and achieve parameter recovery with high probability; in single-index models, the learned feature space aligns the regression signal with specific rates.
conclusion: The work provides a geometric perspective on feature learning in mean-field Langevin dynamics, but it is primarily a machine learning theory paper with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: High-Confidence Minimax Testing With Prescribed Errors
authors: Ilmun Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical minimax lower bounds for testing are typically derived for fixed error probabilities, while high-confidence results often impose a common failure probability. We study prescribed-error testing, in which the level and the target type II error may be small and of different orders. Standard prior-based reductions generally aggregate the two errors into a single quantity and therefore do not capture their distinct roles. We develop a general lower-bound technique based on a binary reduction that preserves the separate roles of the two error targets. The reduction yields two directed Kullback-Leibler information requirements, corresponding respectively to the level and the target type II error. When both directed mixture divergences can be controlled, they combine into a binary Jeffreys divergence, leading to the logarithmic dependence on the level and the target type II error. Applying the framework to Gaussian sequence testing, multinomial uniformity testing, and continuous uniformity testing over H\"older balls, we obtain lower bounds that match corresponding high-confidence upper bounds and hence establish prescribed-error minimax rates sharp up to constant factors.
tldr: This paper develops a general lower-bound technique for prescribed-error testing, deriving minimax rates for Gaussian, multinomial, and continuous uniformity testing.
motivation: Classical minimax lower bounds assume fixed error probabilities, but high-confidence testing often requires separate control of level and type II error, which may be of different orders.
method: The authors propose a binary reduction that preserves the distinct roles of the two error targets, leading to directed Kullback-Leibler information requirements and a Jeffreys divergence bound.
result: The framework yields lower bounds that match high-confidence upper bounds for Gaussian sequence testing, multinomial uniformity testing, and continuous uniformity testing over Hölder balls, establishing sharp minimax rates.
conclusion: The prescribed-error minimax rates are sharp up to constant factors, demonstrating the utility of the proposed technique.

title: A Tunable Incentive Mechanism For Binary Aggregation Without Verification
authors: Wojciech Golab Chien-Chih Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Binary aggregation without verifiable ground truth arises when agents' reports must be aggregated without access to gold-standard labels. This paper studies a tunable reward--penalty mechanism for binary aggregation without verification. Agents choose between a conforming strategy, which reports an informative private signal, and a non-conforming strategy, which follows a deterministic prior-informed report rule. For this mechanism, we derive cost-adjusted sufficient conditions for incentive compatibility and individual rationality as bounds on the reward--penalty ratio. The analysis identifies feasible ratio regions, cases in which ratio adjustment restores feasibility, and parameter regimes in which no ratio satisfies both constraints under the modeled construction. We also state a conditional all-conforming Nash equilibrium result within the restricted strategy set. Entropy-based scaling and stake-weighted redistribution are treated as extensions, with stake-weighted redistribution inducing agent-specific incentive constraints. Numerical checks support the closed-form Tier 1 quantities and illustrate threshold sensitivity.
tldr: This paper proposes a tunable reward-penalty mechanism for binary aggregation without verification, focusing on incentive compatibility and individual rationality.
motivation: Binary aggregation without ground truth is common in crowdsourcing and distributed systems, but existing mechanisms often require verification or lack tunability.
method: The authors model agents' strategies as conforming (reporting private signals) or non-conforming (following a prior-informed rule), and derive bounds on the reward-penalty ratio for incentive compatibility and individual rationality.
result: Feasible ratio regions are identified, and extensions like entropy-based scaling and stake-weighted redistribution are analyzed, with numerical checks supporting the theoretical results.
conclusion: The mechanism can be tuned to satisfy incentive constraints under certain parameter regimes, but the approach is primarily game-theoretic and does not involve quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Witness Complexity Of Short Descriptions: A Cryptographic Perspective
authors: Fabio F. G. Buono
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cryptographic practice, where protocols impose strict time bounds, implementations demand predictable resource usage, and real-world systems require immediate verification for security and usability, a short key or certificate is useful only if it can be expanded or verified within a bounded time; otherwise a compact representation that requires superpolynomial work to expand offers no operational guarantee within a bounded-time protocol. This paper formalises that gap by introducing \(\gam(x)\), the minimum running time over near-shortest descriptions of a string on a universal Turing machine. \(\gam\) differs from Shannon entropy and Kolmogorov complexity \(\KC\): low \(\KC\) can coexist with high \(\gam\). We prove invariance up to polynomial factors; a conditional separation (assuming \(\PneqNP\)). An unconditional lower bound from incomputability of \(\KC\); a biconditional characterisation of \(\PeqNP\) via the class-relative variant \(\gP\); and polynomial-time tractability for structured \(\classNP\) families. Part II develops companion measures and shows an unconditional gap between grammar size and derivation cost, positioning \(\gam\) as a metric for the usability of keys and certificates.
tldr: This paper introduces a new complexity measure for short descriptions from a cryptographic perspective, focusing on the time required to expand or verify compact representations.
motivation: In cryptographic protocols, short keys or certificates are only useful if they can be expanded or verified within bounded time; the paper formalizes the gap between description length and expansion time.
method: The paper defines a function gamma(x) as the minimum running time over near-shortest descriptions on a universal Turing machine, and proves invariance up to polynomial factors, conditional separations assuming P≠NP, and unconditional lower bounds from incomputability of Kolmogorov complexity.
result: It shows that low Kolmogorov complexity can coexist with high gamma, and provides a biconditional characterization of P=NP via a class-relative variant, as well as polynomial-time tractability for structured NP families.
conclusion: The work positions gamma as a metric for the usability of keys and certificates, highlighting that compact representations may not be operationally useful in bounded-time protocols.

title: Power Law Scaling For Classification Accuracy In Physical Neural Networks
authors: Andrei V. Ermolaev, Mathilde Hary, Anas Skalli, Go\"ery Genty, Marcin Gebski, Tomasz Czyszanowski, Stephan Reitzenstein, James A. Lott, John M. Dudley, Daniel Brunner
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical neural networks (PNNs) harness the intrinsic complexity of physical systems to perform neural computation, potentially at speeds and energy efficiencies inaccessible to conventional digital hardware. Yet, a principled framework for quantifying and predicting their computing accuracy across diverse substrates has remained elusive. Here we introduce the Hotelling Trace Criterion (HTC), a task-conditioned measure of PNN- state separability that can be evaluated without training. We demonstrate that it predicts PNN classification performance with high fidelity across highly nonlinear optical fibres, vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers, and coupled nonlinear oscillator networks, for benchmark tasks of different difficulty. Classification loss follows a power law in HTC, with Pearson correlation coefficients exceeding 0.99 for MNIST and [MATH]0.97 for Fashion-MNIST, noteworthy experimental and simulated data from physically distinct systems collapse onto a single scaling curve determined by the task rather than the substrate. Applying HTC layer-by-layer during training further reveals that gradient-based optimisation distributes representational capacity unevenly across PNN layers, providing a quantitative diagnostic of training and architecture efficiency invisible to standard loss monitoring. Crucially, once the scaling exponent is established from a small number of trained calibration systems, all further performance predictions require no training since performance can be derived from the much more efficient HTC measurement. These results establish HTC as a substrate-agnostic figure of merit for comparing and scaling PNNs, advancing the field further towards a complete theory connecting fundamental hardware parameters to task performance through universal scaling laws.
tldr: This paper introduces the Hotelling Trace Criterion (HTC) as a substrate-agnostic measure to predict classification accuracy in physical neural networks without training.
motivation: Physical neural networks (PNNs) lack a principled framework to quantify and predict computing accuracy across diverse substrates, hindering their development.
method: The authors propose the HTC, a task-conditioned measure of PNN state separability evaluated without training, and test it on optical fibers, VCSELs, and coupled oscillator networks.
result: Classification loss follows a power law in HTC with Pearson correlation >0.97 for MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, and data from different substrates collapse onto a single task-dependent scaling curve.
conclusion: HTC serves as a universal figure of merit for PNNs, enabling performance prediction without training once the scaling exponent is calibrated.

title: Digital Signature Schemes Based On Code Equivalence And Syndrome Decoding From Restricted Errors
authors: Sarah Arpin, Jason T. Legrow, Hiram H. L\'opez, Gretchen L. Matthews
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital signature schemes are an important cryptographic tool to ensure data authenticity and integrity in many applications that must be resilient to attacks, including those facilitated by quantum computers. We consider the two digital signature schemes based on error-correcting codes that are second-round candidates in NIST's call for Additional Signature Schemes, which is part of the Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization Process. Specifically, we provide an overview of the Codes and Restricted Objects Signature Scheme (CROSS) and the Linear Equivalence Signature Scheme (LESS). We describe their underlying problems of syndrome decoding from restricted errors and code equivalence. We review sigma protocols and how they can be transformed into digital signature schemes via the Fiat-Shamir transform. Finally, we explain how this procedure yields code-based digital signatures believed to be post-quantum secure.
tldr: This paper reviews two code-based digital signature schemes (CROSS and LESS) that are candidates in NIST's post-quantum cryptography standardization process.
motivation: Digital signatures are essential for data authenticity and integrity, and must be secure against quantum attacks. Code-based cryptography is a promising post-quantum approach.
method: The paper provides an overview of the syndrome decoding from restricted errors and code equivalence problems, describes the sigma protocols underlying CROSS and LESS, and explains how the Fiat-Shamir transform converts them into digital signatures.
result: The paper does not present new results but summarizes existing schemes and their security foundations.
conclusion: CROSS and LESS are believed to be post-quantum secure, but the paper is a survey, not a novel contribution.

title: Exploring Side-Channel Protections In Hardware Implementations Of Pqc Ml-kem Verification
authors: Davis Ranney, Yashaswini I Makaram, A. Adam Ding, Yunsi Fei
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As ML-KEM is adopted as a post-quantum cryptographic standard, resilience against physical side-channel attacks has become essential. Among the constituent steps, the decapsulation Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) verification is particularly vulnerable to side-channel power and electromagnetic (EM) analysis. In this work, we focus on common FPGA-based implementations and examine their side-channel vulnerabilities, and compare them with those of microcontroller implementations. Three verification implementations, unprotected, hash-based (first-order), and higher-order masked, are evaluated for side-channel security on both a microcontroller and an FPGA. While FPGAs offer higher speed and parallelism, they often exhibit stronger side-channel leakage, especially in high bandwidth configurations. The higher-order masked designs still leak information about the underlying data due to hardware-level effects and data-dependent processing. Our experiments show that their parallelized processing on FPGAs introduces sufficient first-order leakage for full secret-key recovery. These results underscore the persistent challenge of securing PQC algorithms in performance-constrained and parallelized hardware environments.
tldr: This paper evaluates side-channel vulnerabilities in hardware implementations of ML-KEM verification, focusing on FPGA and microcontroller platforms.
motivation: ML-KEM is a post-quantum cryptographic standard, and its decapsulation verification is vulnerable to side-channel attacks; securing hardware implementations is critical.
method: Three verification implementations (unprotected, hash-based, higher-order masked) are tested on FPGA and microcontroller using power and EM analysis.
result: FPGA implementations exhibit stronger side-channel leakage, and even higher-order masked designs leak data due to hardware-level effects, enabling full secret-key recovery.
conclusion: Securing PQC algorithms in parallelized hardware environments remains challenging, and current countermeasures are insufficient.

title: Goldblatt-Thomason Theorem For Probability Logic
authors: Somayeh Chopoghloo (school Of Mathematics, Institute For Research In Fundamental Sciences), Massoud Pourmahdian (school Of Mathematics, Institute For Research In Fundamental Sciences), Reihane Zoghifard
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Probability logic (PL) extends propositional logic with countably many probability operators, one for each rational number between 0 and 1. The formulas of this logic are interpreted over the class of Markov processes, i.e., structures of the form [MATH], where[MATH] is a measurable space and [MATH] is a Markov kernel. The main contribution of this paper is the establishment of the Goldblatt-Thomason theorem for probability logic. As an application, we show that the class of Harsanyi type spaces is definable in PL. Moreover, we obtain some variants of the Goldblatt-Thomason theorem for specific subclasses of Markov processes.
tldr: This paper proves a Goldblatt-Thomason theorem for probability logic, characterizing definable classes of Markov processes.
motivation: Probability logic extends propositional logic with probabilistic operators, and the Goldblatt-Thomason theorem is a fundamental result in modal logic that characterizes elementary classes. Establishing it for probability logic provides a deeper understanding of the expressive power and limitations of this logic.
method: The authors use techniques from modal logic and measure theory, defining a notion of bisimulation for Markov processes and showing that a class of Markov processes is definable in probability logic iff it is closed under ultraproducts, ultraroots, and bisimulations.
result: The main result is the Goldblatt-Thomason theorem for probability logic, along with applications to Harsanyi type spaces and variants for subclasses of Markov processes.
conclusion: The paper establishes a key logical characterization for probability logic, which may have implications for the foundations of probabilistic reasoning but does not directly connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Optical Amplification With Large Goos-H$\ddot{a}$nchen Shift Driven By Non-Hermitian Bilayer Meta-Grating
authors: Xueyi Zhang Ma Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical Goos-H[MATH]nchen shifts can be enhanced by resonant mode with high quality factor, such as quasi-bound states in the continuum in meta-grating. Coexistence of gain and loss in bilayer meta-grating with parity-time symmetry could transfer bound states in the continuum into lasing threshold modes with real resonant frequencies and non-zero far-field radiation. When the incident frequency approaches the resonant frequency of a lasing threshold mode, the reflected and transmitted beams are strongly amplified and undergo large Goos-H[MATH]nchen shifts. The amplitude of the Goos-H[MATH]nchen shifts, including the magnitude and sign, are proportional to the reciprocal of the imaginary part of the resonant frequencies. As the incident frequency scan across the resonant frequency of a lasing threshold mode, the imaginary part flip sign, so that the Goos-H[MATH]nchen shifts diverge as well as flip sign. Simulations of optical responses under incident of Gaussian beams with finite beam width exhibit the sign flipping of the Goos-H[MATH]nchen shift with large magnitude by fine tuning the incident frequency across the resonant frequency of a lasing threshold mode.
tldr: This paper studies optical amplification and large Goos-Hänchen shifts in a non-Hermitian bilayer meta-grating with parity-time symmetry.
motivation: To enhance Goos-Hänchen shifts using resonant modes with high quality factor and explore the effects of gain and loss in PT-symmetric structures.
method: The authors design a bilayer meta-grating with parity-time symmetry, analyze lasing threshold modes, and simulate optical responses of Gaussian beams.
result: The Goos-Hänchen shift diverges and flips sign when the incident frequency crosses the resonant frequency of a lasing threshold mode, with amplification.
conclusion: The proposed structure enables large, sign-flipping Goos-Hänchen shifts, which may have applications in optical sensing and switching.

title: On The Structure Of Optimal Free Dirichlet Regions In Mass Transportation Problems
authors: Lucas D. O'brien
abstract: ArXiv:2606.30826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a compactly supported probability measure [MATH] on the [MATH]-dimensional space [MATH], the average distance problem asks us to minimize the average distance functional over all compact, connected, [MATH] satisfying the Hausdorff [MATH]-measure constraint [MATH]. This problem was first introduced in 2002 by Buttazzo, Oudet, and Stepanov to study optimal transport problems with free regions on which the transport cost vanishes, and has undergone a considerable amount of research since. Most recently, Kobayashi, Kim, and the author studied the structure of these regions using the barycentre field, a tool for studying the average distance functional introduced previously by Kobayashi, Hayase, and Kim. In this paper, we build upon this work to prove in much greater generality a topological description of minimizers of the average distance problem conjectured by Buttazzo, Oudet, and Stepanov. In particular, we prove this conjecture in all dimensions in the case originally studied by these authors.
tldr: This paper studies the structure of optimal free Dirichlet regions in mass transportation problems, focusing on the average distance problem.
motivation: The average distance problem was introduced to study optimal transport with free regions where transport cost vanishes, and a conjecture about the topological structure of minimizers remained open.
method: The authors use the barycentre field, a tool for studying the average distance functional, to prove the conjecture in greater generality and in all dimensions.
result: They prove a topological description of minimizers of the average distance problem, confirming the conjecture by Buttazzo, Oudet, and Stepanov.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of optimal free Dirichlet regions in the original setting, advancing the theory of mass transportation problems.

title: Fluid-Antenna-Aided Active User Detection With 1d-cnn Channel Reconstruction For Unsourced Random Access
authors: Haoyu Liang, Zhentian Zhang, Hao Jiang, Jian Dang, Zaichen Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the application of fluid antenna systems (FAS) for active user detection (AUD) in unsourced random access (URA). A channel reconstruction method based on a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) is proposed to effectively learn the nonlinear mapping from partial channel observations to the full channel vector. Furthermore, the reconstructed channel information is exploited to improve AUD performance via port selection. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed 1D-CNN channel reconstructor significantly outperforms traditional methods under varying pilot lengths, achieving superior normalized mean squared error (NMSE) performance. Additionally, the reconstructed channel substantially reduces the AUD error rate compared with conventional approaches relying on traditional antenna configurations.
tldr: This paper applies fluid antenna systems and 1D-CNN for active user detection in unsourced random access, focusing on wireless communication rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Improving active user detection in unsourced random access using fluid antenna systems and deep learning.
method: Proposes a 1D-CNN to reconstruct full channel vectors from partial observations and uses the reconstructed channel for port selection to enhance detection.
result: The 1D-CNN reconstructor achieves lower NMSE and reduces AUD error rate compared to traditional methods.
conclusion: Fluid antenna systems combined with CNN-based channel reconstruction can significantly improve active user detection performance.

title: Periodic Non-uniqueness Sets For Shift-invariant Spaces And Parity-Based Obstructions To The Frame Property For Gabor Systems
authors: Ilya Zlotnikov Alexander Ulanovskii
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The goal of this note is twofold. First, we provide explicit examples of periodic (though not necessarily lattice) sets that give rise to Gabor systems failing to form frames. Our constructions depend only on the parity of the window function [MATH]. Second, for a wide range of finite-dimensional function spaces [MATH] we show that [MATH] contains a function [MATH] such that a lattice of high density fails to generate a Gabor frame. In particular, we prove that the Gr\"ochenig-Lyubarskii theorem is sharp in the finite-dimensional space of polynomials with Gaussian weight. More precisely, for every [MATH] and every [MATH] satisfying [MATH], we give an explicit algorithm for finding an even or odd polynomial [MATH] of degree at most [MATH] such that [MATH] does not form a frame. The proofs are constructive, elementary, and based on linear algebra.
tldr: This paper studies periodic non-uniqueness sets for shift-invariant spaces and parity-based obstructions to Gabor frames, which is a topic in harmonic analysis and frame theory.
motivation: To understand when Gabor systems fail to form frames, and to show sharpness of the Gröchenig-Lyubarskii theorem for finite-dimensional spaces with Gaussian weight.
method: Constructive examples using parity of window functions and linear algebra algorithms for polynomials.
result: Explicit periodic sets and even/odd polynomials are provided that cause Gabor systems to not be frames, even at high lattice densities.
conclusion: The results demonstrate fundamental limitations in Gabor frame constructions and highlight the role of parity and periodicity.

title: Gaussian Belief Propagation For Tracking With Unresolved Measurements
authors: Augustin A. Saucan, Florian Meyer, Peter Willett
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unresolved measurements occur in many inference problems where two or more hidden processes may, at times, jointly generate a single measurement. For instance, such phenomena are encountered in multiobject tracking owing to the limited resolution capabilities of practical sensors; or in camera-aided autonomous driving due to shadowing or occlusions. Substantial performance degradation, such as track losses, are incurred when unresolved measurements are not accounted for. In this paper, we address multiobject tracking under a generalized unresolved measurement model, where any subset of objects may generate a single unresolved measurement according to a probabilistic model. Our innovation lies both in modeling and algorithm-design directions. First, we develop a probability distribution for object partitions based on a model of pairwise coupling of objects and subsequently a probability distribution for object-to-measurement association variables. This generic model incorporates sensor resolution capabilities, sensor detection, and sensor noise characteristics for object groups. Second, a generic Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) method as well as a specialized Gaussian-LBP (GLBP) algorithm are proposed that perform object state inference under the aforementioned model. In contrast to direct marginalization methods, which involve a computational complexity of [MATH], for [MATH] measurements and [MATH] objects, the proposed GLBP algorithm achieves a computational complexity on the order of [MATH]. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed GLBP, with estimation performance that closely matches that of exact marginalization for only a fraction of the computational resources.
tldr: This paper proposes a Gaussian Belief Propagation algorithm for multiobject tracking with unresolved measurements, focusing on computational efficiency.
motivation: Unresolved measurements in multiobject tracking cause performance degradation; existing methods are computationally expensive.
method: The authors develop a probabilistic model for object partitions and measurement associations, then propose a Loopy Belief Propagation method and a specialized Gaussian-LBP algorithm for inference.
result: The GLBP algorithm achieves computational complexity O(NM) compared to exponential complexity of exact methods, with estimation performance close to exact marginalization.
conclusion: The proposed GLBP algorithm effectively handles unresolved measurements in multiobject tracking with significantly reduced computational cost.

title: The Cooperation Ceiling: Extrinsic Population Dynamics And The Intrinsic Escape
authors: Harry Foster, Vince Knight, Sebastian Krapohl
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolutionary game theory provides a framework by which to study the emergence of cooperation in a population of self-interested actors. In such a framework, players' decisions on whether or not to cooperate evolve according to decision rules called population dynamics. However, often games are studied under the assumption that all individuals play under the same conditions, and many common choices of update rule are not well suited for a heterogeneous population. In this paper, we categorise and compare four different population dynamics in such a population as ``extrinsic'', where players learn by looking outward at the payoffs of other players, and ``intrinsic'', where players look inwardly at their own attributes or potential payoffs. We show that extrinsic population dynamics admit a ceiling on the rate of cooperation which can be exceeded by intrinsic population dynamics, and demonstrate this using the public goods game with heterogeneous contributions.
tldr: This paper studies cooperation in evolutionary game theory using extrinsic and intrinsic population dynamics, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding cooperation in heterogeneous populations is a classic problem in evolutionary game theory.
method: The authors categorize and compare four population dynamics (extrinsic vs intrinsic) and test them in a public goods game with heterogeneous contributions.
result: Extrinsic dynamics impose a ceiling on cooperation rates, while intrinsic dynamics can exceed that ceiling.
