We present AI-Infra-Guard, an open-source framework that organizes AI red teaming around a single observation: the attack surface of an AI agent is stratified across layers (infrastructure, protocol/tool, agent behavior, and model), and no single detection paradigm fits all of them. The framework therefore matches a paradigm to each layer, from deterministic rule matching over 75+ AI components and 1{,}400+ vulnerability rules, through LLM-driven agentic auditing of MCP servers and agent-skill packages and multi-turn black-box agent red teaming, to a jailbreak harness with 26+ attack operators over sixteen datasets. To our knowledge it is the only open-source framework to span all of these, including supply-chain auditing of the agent skills that increasingly extend AI agents. We release AI-Infra-Guard as open source so that can serve as a practical foundation for agent security and a shared base for the community to build on.
tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for red-teaming AI agents across multiple security layers.
motivation: The rapid growth of open-source AI infrastructure has outpaced security tooling, necessitating a comprehensive red-teaming framework.
method: The framework stratifies the attack surface into infrastructure, protocol/tool, agent behavior, and model layers, and applies tailored detection paradigms (rule matching, LLM-driven auditing, multi-turn black-box testing, jailbreak harness) to each.
result: The framework covers over 75 AI components and 1,400+ vulnerability rules, and includes supply-chain auditing for agent skills.
conclusion: AI-Infra-Guard is the first open-source framework to span all these layers, providing a practical foundation for agent security.

title: The Decomposition Is The Fingerprint: Per-Component Identity For Agent Skills
authors: Hongliang Liu, Yuhao Wu, Tung-Ling Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly acquire and execute skills at runtime: bundles of prompt instructions, executable code, and tool declarations fetched from marketplaces and other agents. Governing them needs a stable notion of skill identity, yet cryptographic hashing is engineered to destroy the very similarity we need, as a one-character edit scrambles the digest. We present a compact, locality-sensitive fingerprint that embeds each component of a skill and projects it to bits with a multi-bank SimHash, giving a fixed 120-byte signature compared in constant time by Hamming distance. Our central claim is that keeping the fingerprint as a per-component triple (prompt, code, tools), rather than a single score, is what makes it useful: the triple recovers skill-family identity through paraphrase, renaming, refactoring, and controlled code translation when another component remains shared, while independent multilingual reimplementation is not recovered; it also localizes which component carries the reuse. We claim lineage, not behavioral equivalence: identity supplies the structural axis of a registry and leaves safety to behavioral verification. The fingerprint reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.974 (95% CI [0.956, 0.994]) over 4,950 pairwise comparisons while using 77x fewer bits than the embedding it approximates, with ranking preserved in expectation and finite-bit concentration; the per-component split turns one number into relationship classification, families, novelty, and a portable "SkillBOM" for a skill registry. On a 906-skill injection benchmark the fingerprint recognizes injected skills as tampered copies of a known base and localizes the change, but recognition is not trust: it remains, by design, an identity signal complementary to behavioral verification rather than a safety verdict.
tldr: The paper proposes a locality-sensitive fingerprint for AI agent skills to enable similarity detection and lineage tracking, but it is unrelated to quantum information theory or quantum thermodynamics.
motivation: AI agents need a stable notion of skill identity for governance, but cryptographic hashing destroys similarity information.
method: A multi-bank SimHash generates a 120-byte fingerprint per skill component (prompt, code, tools), compared by Hamming distance.
result: The fingerprint achieves AUC 0.974 on pairwise comparisons, uses 77x fewer bits than embeddings, and localizes changes in injected skills.
conclusion: The fingerprint provides a structural identity signal for skill registries, complementary to behavioral verification.

title: Learning Fair Allocation Of Indivisible Items From Limited Feedback
authors: Xinyu Liu, David Kempe, Evi Micha
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a setting in which an algorithm must output a fair allocation of indivisible items while "learning on the job". More specifically, the algorithm is to output an allocation satisfying EF1, PROP1, or similar fairness notions; however, the algorithm initially has no information about the agents' valuations, and can only learn about them by (repeatedly) proposing an allocation, and obtaining feedback about a fairness violation in the allocation. Importantly, the observed fairness violation may be adversarially chosen. The algorithm's goal is to converge to a fair allocation in rounds polynomial in the number of agents and items, ideally with only polynomial computation. We prove two main results: first, when the valuations are additive, then even for mixed items (goods and chores), an allocation satisfying EF1 or PROP1 can be found in polynomial time using the corresponding feedback. These results are instantiations of a more general framework which maintains a polytope of candidate valuations consistent with all past feedback. The algorithm repeatedly constructs putative valuations and uses them to propose allocations; the observed violations then define separating hyperplanes, allowing the algorithm to emulate the ellipsoid method. When the valuations are monotone, we present an algorithm which is guaranteed to find an EF1 allocation in polynomially many iterations; however, its internal calculations are not guaranteed to be polynomial. The algorithm again maintains putative valuations, and only considers allocations in which each agent obtains an interval plus one additional item with respect to an arbitrary ordering of the items. We (non-constructively) prove that there always exist EF1 allocations of this form, allowing us to use a further generalization of the preceding ellipsoid-based ideas.
tldr: This paper studies learning fair allocations of indivisible items from limited feedback, focusing on EF1 and PROP1 notions.
motivation: The algorithm must output a fair allocation without prior knowledge of agent valuations, learning only through feedback on proposed allocations.
method: The algorithm maintains a polytope of candidate valuations consistent with feedback, uses the ellipsoid method to converge to a fair allocation.
result: For additive valuations, an EF1 or PROP1 allocation can be found in polynomial time; for monotone valuations, an EF1 allocation is guaranteed in polynomially many iterations but with potentially non-polynomial internal computation.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical guarantees for learning fair allocations under limited feedback, but is not related to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Cve-ttp Kg: Knowledge Graph Linking Software Vulnerabilities To Attack Behaviors
authors: Basant Agarwal, Dincy R. Arikkat, Swati Yadav, Serena Nicolazzo, Antonino Nocera, Vinod P
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the evolving threat landscape, adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities to launch sophisticated attacks, challenging traditional defenses. Although databases like CVE and NVD provide detailed technical information, they often lack links to attacker behaviors such as tactics and techniques, limiting effective threat interpretation and response. This work bridges this gap by connecting vulnerabilities with behavioral patterns from the MITRE ATT&CK framework. We construct a CVE-TTP Knowledge Graph that links CVEs to tactics and techniques using classification and relation extraction. Transformer-based models are developed for behavior identification, with CySecBERT achieving macro F1-scores of 87.71% (techniques) and 96.16% (tactics). Also, we created an annotated dataset with 24,820 entities and 43,608 relations for entity and relation extraction. The pipeline-based approach achieves macro F1-scores of 0.86 (entity extraction) and 0.99 (relation extraction), while a span-based joint model achieves 0.78. These outputs are integrated into a Neo4j-based Cyber Threat Knowledge Graph, enabling structured visualization of vulnerabilities.
tldr: This paper constructs a knowledge graph linking software vulnerabilities (CVEs) to attacker behaviors (MITRE ATT&CK) using NLP and relation extraction.
motivation: Traditional vulnerability databases lack connections to attacker tactics and techniques, hindering threat interpretation and response.
method: Transformer-based models (CySecBERT) classify CVEs into tactics/techniques; pipeline and joint models extract entities and relations to build a Neo4j knowledge graph.
result: CySecBERT achieves macro F1-scores of 87.71% for techniques and 96.16% for tactics; entity extraction F1=0.86, relation extraction F1=0.99.
conclusion: The CVE-TTP knowledge graph effectively links vulnerabilities to attack behaviors, enabling structured threat analysis.

title: Comparative Analysis Of Machine Learning Based Intrusion Detection In Realistic IoT Networks
authors: Chuadhry Mujeeb Ahmed Rana Alharbi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly growing and expanding into various sectors, such as healthcare, transportation, smart homes, and more. Despite the benefits of using IoT devices, they present several challenges. Given the significant role these devices play in our lives, it is crucial to address issues related to their security and privacy. These devices are limited in resources, which complicates their security and the protection of the data that they manage. The paper aims to examine intrusion detection systems using the Gotham2025 dataset, generated through the Gotham testbed, which consists of 78 emulated IoT devices utilising various protocols, including MQTT, CoAP, and RTSP, to assist in safeguarding IoT networks from attacks. We conduct a comparative analysis between five machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, and Deep Neural Network. We demonstrate that the Random Forest Classifier was the top-performing model, achieving an F1-score of 0.99 in classifying attacks.
tldr: This paper compares machine learning algorithms for intrusion detection in IoT networks using the Gotham2025 dataset.
motivation: IoT devices are resource-constrained and vulnerable to attacks, necessitating effective intrusion detection systems.
method: Five machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Deep Neural Network) are evaluated on the Gotham2025 dataset from a testbed of 78 emulated IoT devices.
result: Random Forest achieved the highest F1-score of 0.99 in classifying attacks.
conclusion: Machine learning, particularly Random Forest, can effectively detect intrusions in IoT networks.

title: Robocalls: A Worldwide Or US-only Problem? Analyzing Spam And Fraud In International Phone Calls
authors: Kemal Altwlkany, Andro Mer\'cep, Tomislav {\dj}uri\v{c}i\'c, Ante Kapetanovi\'c, Emanuel Lacic
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unsolicited automated phone calls (robocalls) are a serious threat: in the US alone, these calls resulted in reported losses of 1.1$ billion during 2025. Phishing and spoofing consistently rank among the most reported crimes within the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, with phone call scams having the highest reported median loss. Combating robocalls is difficult due to many legal and practical constraints: robocalls often encompass multiple legal jurisdictions of different countries/states, the large volume of robocalls, their multilingual nature, the lack of publicly available data, privacy concerns with obtaining data, etc. We present a study of international robocalls, aggregating robocall reports from countries across all inhabited continents and contribute by providing new findings on international robocalls from 65 different countries. We also present the first publicly available multimodal and international robocall dataset: 8.7 million call detail records, 839 robocall transcripts from 28 identified robocall campaign clusters, and 677 robocall recordings. We describe our methodology for collecting robocall data over a 9-month period and provide a detailed analysis comparing robocalls in the US with those in other countries. Our analysis covers several aspects, including uncovering calling patterns, identifying co-targeting attacks, discovering common robocall campaigns, extracting callback numbers, analyzing linguistic differences among robocalls in the same language but different regions, and other insights. Our results indicate that although robocalls are an international problem, the severity of the threat is significantly higher in the US than in other countries. We provide steps for future research and suggest remedies to reduce the effectiveness of robocalls based on our analysis.
tldr: This paper analyzes international robocall patterns and presents a multimodal dataset of robocalls from 65 countries.
motivation: Robocalls cause significant financial losses and are difficult to combat due to legal and practical constraints; the study aims to understand the international scope and characteristics of robocalls.
method: The authors collected 8.7 million call detail records, 839 transcripts, and 677 recordings over 9 months from multiple countries, and performed comparative analysis between US and non-US robocalls.
result: Robocalls are an international problem but the threat severity is significantly higher in the US than in other countries.
conclusion: The findings suggest that while robocalls are global, US-specific measures may be needed, and the dataset can support future research on combating robocalls.

title: Counting Small Induced Subgraphs: Hardness Of Symmetry-Based Properties
authors: Mingjun Liu Radu Curticapean
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jerrum and Meeks (TOCT, JCSS 2015) introduced the counting problems [MATH] for fixed graph properties [MATH]: Given an input graph [MATH] and [MATH], count the [MATH]-vertex subsets [MATH] such that the induced subgraph [MATH] satisfies [MATH]. For recursively enumerable [MATH], it is known that [MATH] is either #W[1]-hard or fixed-parameter tractable. A direct classification depending on [MATH] however still remains open. In particular, the status was open for the property of graphs without nontrivial automorphisms, also mentioned in a very recent survey on parameterized counting by Roth (Comput.~Sci.~Rev.~2026). This is a natural property that evades all currently known techniques for proving #W[1]-hardness, including a general toolkit based on Fourier analysis that was very recently introduced by Curticapean and Neuen (SODA~2025). In this paper, we show that counting induced [MATH]-vertex graphs without nontrivial automorphisms is #W[1]-hard by constructing ``clique scaffolds'', i.e., problem-specific restrictions of the property that enable a reduction from the [MATH]-clique problem. More generally, we show that for every finite group [MATH], counting [MATH]-vertex induced subgraphs with automorphism group [MATH] is #W[1]-hard.
tldr: This paper proves #W[1]-hardness of counting induced subgraphs with no nontrivial automorphisms, using clique scaffolds.
motivation: The problem of counting induced subgraphs with a given property is fundamental in parameterized complexity, and the status for the property of having no nontrivial automorphisms was open.
method: The authors construct 'clique scaffolds', which are problem-specific restrictions that enable a reduction from the k-clique problem.
result: Counting induced k-vertex subgraphs without nontrivial automorphisms is #W[1]-hard, and more generally, for any finite group G, counting induced subgraphs with automorphism group G is #W[1]-hard.
conclusion: The paper resolves an open problem in parameterized counting complexity, showing hardness for a natural symmetry-based property.

title: Labelled Sequent Calculi For Propositional Team Logics
authors: Fausto Barbero, Marianna Girlando, Valentin M\"uller, Fan Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Team semantics is a general framework where formulas are not interpreted with respect to a single point of evaluation, but with respect to sets of such points. Team semantics is used in dependence logic, to reason about dependencies between variables, and in inquisitive logic, to formalize the meaning of questions. We provide sound and complete labelled sequent calculi for four logics based on team semantics: basic inquisitive logic, propositional intuitionistic dependence logic, and their respective extensions with tensor disjunction. For technical reasons, we restrict ourselves to languages with finitely many propositional atoms. The rules of weakening, contraction and cut are shown to be admissible in each of our calculi. In the last part of the paper, we present terminating proof search procedures for variants of our proof systems, in which labels have a simplified structure.
tldr: The paper presents sound and complete labelled sequent calculi for propositional team logics, including inquisitive logic and dependence logic.
motivation: Team semantics provides a framework for reasoning about dependencies and questions, but proof-theoretic foundations for these logics were lacking.
method: The authors develop labelled sequent calculi for four team-based logics, prove admissibility of structural rules, and provide terminating proof search procedures.
result: Sound and complete labelled sequent calculi are obtained for basic inquisitive logic, propositional intuitionistic dependence logic, and their extensions with tensor disjunction.
conclusion: The work establishes a proof-theoretic foundation for team logics, enabling automated reasoning and further meta-theoretic studies.

title: Belief Contraction In Dynamic Epistemic Logic
authors: Snow Zhang Gaia Belardinelli (stanford University)
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic epistemic logic represents belief change via model transformations induced by epistemic events. Its standard formulation (Baltag, Moss, Solecki, 1998) provides a natural account of belief expansion through the elimination of possibilities, but it cannot model belief contraction about factual propositions. A classic response enriches Kripke models with plausibility orderings, representing contraction as an update that promotes certain possibilities over others. We show that this approach has expressive limitations. In particular, the approach cannot model belief that violates positive introspection and contraction dynamics in response to a hedged public announcement that phi might be false. Motivated by these considerations, we introduce a mechanism for belief contraction defined directly on standard Kripke models, without any constraints on the doxastic accessibility relation. We show that it satisfies some of the standard properties of belief contraction but not others, study the conditions under which contraction may be unsuccessful, and provide a sound and complete axiomatization of the logic via reduction axioms. We also define a more general dynamic logic that is an extension of standard DEL and accommodates belief contractions due to events such as private or semi-private announcements, and provide a complete and sound axiomatization of the general logic.
tldr: This paper proposes a mechanism for belief contraction in dynamic epistemic logic, addressing limitations of existing approaches that rely on plausibility orderings.
motivation: Standard dynamic epistemic logic cannot model belief contraction about factual propositions, and existing solutions using plausibility orderings have expressive limitations, such as inability to model violations of positive introspection or hedged public announcements.
method: The authors introduce a belief contraction mechanism defined directly on standard Kripke models without constraints on the doxastic accessibility relation, and extend it to a general dynamic logic accommodating private or semi-private announcements, providing sound and complete axiomatizations via reduction axioms.
result: The proposed contraction satisfies some standard properties but not others; conditions for unsuccessful contraction are studied, and the logic is fully axiomatized.
conclusion: The work provides a novel approach to belief contraction in dynamic epistemic logic, but it is purely in the domain of philosophical logic and does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Most Properties Are Undecidable For Transitive Tense Logics
authors: Qian Chen (the Tsinghua-Uva JRC For Logic, Department Of Philosophy, Tsinghua University), Tenyo Takahashi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A logics' property is decidable in a class of logics if there exists an algorithm that decides whether a finitely axiomatizable logic in the class has the property. Many properties are undecidable for bimodal logics but decidable for linear tense logics, which leads to a general question on how the interactions of modalities affect the decidability of properties. In this paper, we study the decidability of properties for transitive tense logics and show that most properties are undecidable in the lattice NExt(K4t) of transitive tense logics, including Kripke completeness, the finite model property, and decidability. Our proof method adapts Chagrov's approach of constructing a reduction from an undecidable problem of Minsky machines to the decision problem for logics' properties, yielding a general scheme of proving the undecidability of these properties.
tldr: This paper proves undecidability of many properties for transitive tense logics using a reduction from Minsky machines.
motivation: To understand how interactions of modalities affect decidability of properties in bimodal logics, specifically transitive tense logics.
method: Adapts Chagrov's approach to construct a reduction from an undecidable problem of Minsky machines to the decision problem for logics' properties.
result: Shows that Kripke completeness, the finite model property, and decidability are undecidable in the lattice NExt(K4t) of transitive tense logics.
conclusion: Most properties are undecidable for transitive tense logics, extending known undecidability results from bimodal logics.

title: Labelled Sequents For Inquisitive First-Order Modal Logic
authors: Simone Conti Ivano Ciardelli (university Of Padua)
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent work, an inquisitive first-order modal logic has been proposed to reason about relations of modal dependence, including the notion of global supervenience (functional dependence among the extensions of predicates relative to a space of possibilities). At present, no proof system exists for this logic. We provide a complete labelled sequent calculus, extending a calculus developed by Litak and Sano for a weak version of inquisitive first-order logic. We prove strong completeness for the calculus and show that it enjoys desirable structural properties, including the invertibility of its rules and the admissibility of cut.
tldr: This paper presents a labelled sequent calculus for inquisitive first-order modal logic, focusing on proof theory and completeness.
motivation: Inquisitive first-order modal logic was proposed to reason about modal dependence and supervenience, but no proof system existed.
method: The authors extend a labelled sequent calculus by Litak and Sano, proving strong completeness and structural properties like invertibility and cut admissibility.
result: A complete labelled sequent calculus is provided with desirable structural properties.
conclusion: The calculus fills a gap in proof theory for inquisitive modal logic, but the work is purely logical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Intuitionistic Monotone Modal Logic: Proof Theory And Semantics
authors: Jim de Groot Tiziano Dalmonte
abstract: ArXiv:2606.31870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the recently introduced intuitionistic monotone modal logic IM. We first provide a semantic characterisation for a family of natural extensions of IM in terms of constructive neighbourhood models. We then present a calculus for IM and its extensions, obtained by adapting a structured calculus for the classical monotone modal logic M. Based on the calculus, we prove some preliminary results for IM, including its decidability. Our calculus also reveals an interesting analogy between constructive and intuitionistic variants of M and the corresponding variants of K, thereby further justifying IM as a faithful intuitionistic variant of M.
tldr: This paper studies intuitionistic monotone modal logic, providing a semantic characterization and a calculus for the logic and its extensions.
motivation: The authors aim to fill a gap in the study of intuitionistic modal logics by investigating the monotone variant, which has not been thoroughly explored.
method: They use constructive neighbourhood models for semantics and adapt a structured calculus from classical monotone modal logic to the intuitionistic setting.
result: They prove decidability for the basic logic and some extensions, and reveal an analogy between constructive and intuitionistic variants of monotone modal logic and the corresponding variants of normal modal logic.
conclusion: The work justifies intuitionistic monotone modal logic as a faithful intuitionistic counterpart of classical monotone modal logic, but the results are purely logical and not connected to quantum information or thermodynamics.
